lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The 24 English consonant sounds: place, manner, voicing and examples
objectives: Identify the 24 consonant phonemes in one consistent British English teaching model.
Classify each consonant by place of articulation, manner of articulation and voicing.
Recognise two checked example words for each consonant phoneme.
Use IPA symbols accurately and distinguish English /r/ from the IPA alveolar trill, and /j/ from a voiceless sound.
Complete a keyed exercise giving two example words for each of ten specified consonants.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL TEACHING — The 24 consonant phonemes in a British English teaching model

A consonant is described by three main features:
• Place of articulation: where the airflow is narrowed or stopped in the vocal tract.
• Manner of articulation: how the airflow is stopped, narrowed or allowed to pass.
• Voicing: whether the vocal folds vibrate. Put two fingers lightly on the front of your throat: you can often feel vibration for a voiced sound and not for its voiceless partner. This is a simple demonstration, not a pronunciation assessment.

The table below uses one consistent British English teaching model with 24 consonant phonemes. The examples show the sound, not just the spelling. A phoneme may be written with one symbol (/p/) or two symbols (/tʃ/, /dʒ/); the latter are single affricate phonemes in this model. Accent variation exists, so do not assume every English speaker uses an identical inventory or pronunciation.

| IPA sound | Place | Manner | Voicing | Two example words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| /p/ | bilabial (both lips) | plosive | voiceless | pen, cap |
| /b/ | bilabial | plosive | voiced | bad, rub |
| /t/ | alveolar (tongue at the ridge behind upper teeth) | plosive | voiceless | tea, set |
| /d/ | alveolar | plosive | voiced | day, red |
| /k/ | velar (back of tongue at soft palate) | plosive | voiceless | key, take |
| /ɡ/ | velar | plosive | voiced | get, rug |
| /f/ | labiodental (lower lip and upper teeth) | fricative | voiceless | fine, life |
| /v/ | labiodental | fricative | voiced | van, love |
| /θ/ | dental (tongue at or near teeth) | fricative | voiceless | thin, bath |
| /ð/ | dental | fricative | voiced | this, then |
| /s/ | alveolar | fricative | voiceless | soon, bus |
| /z/ | alveolar | fricative | voiced | zero, days |
| /ʃ/ | postalveolar (just behind the alveolar ridge) | fricative | voiceless | ship, wish |
| /ʒ/ | postalveolar | fricative | voiced | vision, pleasure |
| /h/ | glottal (at the vocal folds) | fricative | voiceless | hat, behind |
| /tʃ/ | postalveolar | affricate (stop followed by frication) | voiceless | chain, catch |
| /dʒ/ | postalveolar | affricate | voiced | jam, bridge |
| /m/ | bilabial | nasal | voiced | milk, come |
| /n/ | alveolar | nasal | voiced | nice, on |
| /ŋ/ | velar | nasal | voiced | sing, long |
| /l/ | alveolar | lateral approximant | voiced | light, hole |
| /r/ (often realised [ɹ]) | postalveolar | approximant | voiced | red, carry |
| /j/ | palatal (front of tongue near hard palate) | approximant | voiced | yes, young |
| /w/ | labio-velar (lips rounded, back of tongue raised) | approximant | voiced | wet, well |

MANNER GROUPS
1. Plosives /p b t d k ɡ/: the airflow is briefly stopped and then released.
2. Fricatives /f v θ ð s z ʃ ʒ h/: air passes through a narrow opening and creates friction.
3. Affricates /tʃ dʒ/: a stop release moves directly into frication; each is treated as one consonant phoneme here.
4. Nasals /m n ŋ/: the mouth is closed at the place of articulation and air passes through the nose.
5. Approximants /l r j w/: the articulators approach one another without the strong friction of a fricative. /l/ is lateral because air passes around the sides of the tongue.

VOICING PAIRS
The following pairs differ mainly in voicing: /p/–/b/, /t/–/d/, /k/–/ɡ/, /f/–/v/, /θ/–/ð/, /s/–/z/, /ʃ/–/ʒ/, and /tʃ/–/dʒ/. The first sound in each pair is voiceless; the second is voiced. The remaining consonants in this 24-sound model are voiced except /h/, which is voiceless.

IMPORTANT IPA AND SOURCE CORRECTIONS
The International Phonetic Association chart arranges consonants by place and manner; where a pair shares a cell, the symbol on the right is voiced and the one on the left is voiceless. Do not treat ordinary letter shapes as IPA symbols. The English /r/ phoneme is commonly written /r/ in broad learner transcriptions; its usual British sound is the postalveolar approximant [ɹ], not the IPA alveolar trill [r]. The /j/ in yes is a voiced palatal approximant, not a voiceless sound. The /t/ in tea is alveolar, not velar; /k/ is velar. The affricates /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ are single phonemes in this model, not two unrelated consonants.

The source's Week 7 table contains incorrect place/voicing labels and doubtful or non-IPA lookalikes in its examples. Those defects remain recorded against the original source; this newly authored table supplies a checked teaching reference rather than rewriting the source. The word examples are checked against established British pronunciation guides. This lesson assesses classification and example recognition only. It does not claim to assess a learner's spoken performance; oral pronunciation assessment and audio evidence remain deferred.

practice.question: Give two example words for each of these ten consonant sounds: /p/, /b/, /t/, /k/, /f/, /θ/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/, /m/ and /ŋ/. Use words in which the target sound is clearly present. (20 marks)
practice.answer: /p/: pen, cap. /b/: bad, rub. /t/: tea, set. /k/: key, take. /f/: fine, life. /θ/: thin, bath. /ʃ/: ship, wish. /tʃ/: chain, catch. /m/: milk, come. /ŋ/: sing, long.

practice.question: Classify these four sounds by place, manner and voicing: /p/, /v/, /ŋ/ and /dʒ/. (12 marks)
practice.answer: /p/: bilabial, plosive, voiceless. /v/: labiodental, fricative, voiced. /ŋ/: velar, nasal, voiced. /dʒ/: postalveolar, affricate, voiced.

marking.criterion: /p/ has correct place, manner and voicing
/v/ has correct place, manner and voicing
/ŋ/ has correct place, manner and voicing
/dʒ/ has correct place, manner and voicing

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Narrative writing: a worked plan, model ending and 20-mark rubric
objectives: Plan a narrative with a setting, characters, opening, complication, rising action, climax, resolution and moral.
Develop a logical sequence of events using relevant detail and consistent tense.
Study an original model story whose complete ending expresses the moral 'It pays to be hardworking'.
Write an original story with the required moral without copying the model scene.
Apply a transparent 20-mark rubric to an original student narrative.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL TEACHING — Planning and writing a narrative with a clear moral

A narrative tells a sequence of events involving people in a particular setting. A strong story has a beginning that introduces the situation, a complication that creates a problem, rising action that develops the problem, a climax where the main difficulty is faced, and a resolution that shows what happens afterwards. The events should connect logically. Use dialogue sparingly, choose details that help the reader imagine the scene, and keep the tense and point of view consistent.

WORKED PLAN
Title: The School Radio Broadcast

Setting: A secondary school's media room during the week of its annual showcase.
Main character: Amina, a pupil who volunteers to prepare the school's short radio bulletin.
Other characters: Mr Bello, the media-club teacher; Chika, Amina's partner.
Opening situation: The team is asked to produce a clear three-minute bulletin for the showcase. Their first recording has a crackling microphone and an overlong script.
Complication: The showcase is only five days away. Chika thinks the team should abandon the recording and read the notices aloud without preparation.
Rising action: Amina divides the work into short tasks, edits the script, checks names and times against the school noticeboard, practises reading at a steady pace, and asks Mr Bello to show them how to test the microphone cable. The first two recordings still contain mistakes, so she marks the problem sections and tries again.
Climax: During the final rehearsal, the microphone becomes noisy again. Instead of blaming Chika, Amina checks the cable connection, changes to the spare microphone and restarts the bulletin from the last clear sentence.
Resolution: The final recording is accurate, easy to hear and exactly three minutes long. The media club plays it at the showcase, and the audience understands every announcement.
Reflection/moral: Amina learns that steady preparation and patient effort turn a difficult task into a successful one. The story ends with the exact moral: “It pays to be hardworking.”

MODEL STORY — The School Radio Broadcast
On Monday morning, Mr Bello announced that the media club would prepare a three-minute radio bulletin for the school's annual showcase. Amina and Chika volunteered. They were excited until their first recording sounded like a voice speaking through a storm. The script was also so long that it lasted nearly six minutes.

“We can just read the notices on the day,” Chika suggested. “There is no time to fix everything.”

Amina looked at the calendar. The showcase was five days away. She divided the work into small tasks. First, she shortened the script. Next, she checked every name, date and time against the noticeboard. She and Chika practised reading each item clearly, without rushing. Mr Bello showed them how to test the microphone cable and keep the microphone at a steady distance. Their second recording was shorter, but Amina noticed that one announcement had the wrong starting time. She corrected it and practised again.

On Friday, the team began its final rehearsal. Halfway through the bulletin, the microphone crackled and the sound disappeared. Chika sighed. Amina did not argue. She checked the cable, connected the spare microphone and returned to the last sentence that had been recorded clearly. They began again. This time, every word was audible and the bulletin ended after exactly three minutes.

At the showcase, the audience listened without confusion. Several pupils said the announcements were easy to follow, and Mr Bello thanked both club members for their careful work. Chika smiled at Amina. “I thought we should give up,” he admitted, “but your plan helped us finish.” Amina was pleased, not because everything had been easy, but because she had kept working when the first attempts failed. She had learned that effort, patience and careful checking matter. It pays to be hardworking.

HOW TO USE THE RUBRIC
The rubric below is for a learner's own story on the same moral. The model story is an example of planning and revision, not a text to copy. A learner may choose a different setting, characters and problem. The story must be original and must end with the required moral sentence.

| Criterion | What the marker looks for | Marks |
|---|---|---:|
| Relevance to task | Story is a narrative and leads naturally to the required moral | 2 |
| Plot structure | Clear opening, complication, rising action and climax/resolution | 4 |
| Characters and setting | People and place are established and remain understandable | 2 |
| Hard work shown | Specific repeated effort, practice or persistence affects the outcome | 3 |
| Details and dialogue | Relevant descriptive detail or dialogue helps the reader follow events | 2 |
| Ending and moral | Resolution is complete and final sentence is exactly “It pays to be hardworking.” | 2 |
| Organisation | Paragraphs and time links make the sequence easy to follow | 2 |
| Language accuracy | Grammar, spelling and punctuation are clear enough to communicate the story | 3 |
| TOTAL |  | 20 |

For fair marking, award marks only for evidence in the submitted story. Do not award the hard-work marks merely because the moral sentence is copied at the end; the events must show effort. Do not penalise a learner for choosing a different story from the model.

practice.question: From the worked plan, list the five main stages in the event sequence, from the opening situation to the resolution. (5 marks)
practice.answer: (1) The media club is asked to prepare a three-minute bulletin. (2) The first recording is noisy and too long. (3) Amina divides the work, edits and checks the script, and practises. (4) The microphone fails during the final rehearsal; Amina changes to the spare microphone and restarts. (5) The final bulletin is clear and plays successfully at the showcase.

practice.question: Write your own original narrative about a person whose effort leads to a worthwhile result. Plan the events before writing. Your final sentence must be exactly: “It pays to be hardworking.” Use the 20-mark rubric in the lesson. (20 marks)
practice.answer: Responses will vary. A complete response must be an original narrative, not a retelling of the model; it must show effort through specific actions, develop a clear sequence and resolution, and end with the exact required moral. Apply the rubric criterion by criterion.

marking.criterion: complete ending and exact moral sentence

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Contextual word meanings: man, appreciate, debt, forgiveness and rail
objectives: Use sentence context and part of speech to distinguish the noun and verb senses of man.
Check the verb man in a reliable dictionary and distinguish it from guide and manage.
Choose context-appropriate synonyms for appreciate, debt and forgiveness.
Distinguish the verb rail (complain angrily) from the noun rail (a support bar or a railway track), using clear sentence contexts.
lessons.body:
Words do not always keep one meaning in every sentence. The surrounding words and the situation help us decide which sense is intended. To work out a meaning, read the whole sentence, identify the word's part of speech, suggest a meaning that fits, and test it by replacing the word. A replacement is suitable only if the sentence still makes sense and keeps its original idea.

The word man can be a noun or a verb. In “That man is my father”, man is a noun: it names an adult male person. In “Security officers man the gate”, man is a verb: the officers are present to staff and operate the gate. In “Volunteers man the telephone lines”, they are present to answer the calls. The verb is normally used with an object: a person or team mans a post, station, telephone line or piece of equipment. Its forms are man, mans, manned and manning.

A dictionary check matters because a guessed synonym can teach the wrong meaning. The source note glosses “man the gate” as “guide” and “man the office” as “take charge, or manage”. Those are not precise dictionary equivalents. To man a gate is to staff the post and be present to operate or control it; to man an office is to staff or work at that office. It does not automatically mean to guide someone, own the office or manage the whole organisation. If the intended meaning is “show someone the way”, use guide; if it is “direct the organisation”, use manage. In many situations, staff or operate is clearer and avoids the gendered wording of man as a verb.

A word may also have more than one sense while keeping the same part of speech. Appreciate is a verb. In “I appreciate your help”, it means value the help or feel grateful for it. In “We appreciate how difficult the task is”, it means understand or recognise the difficulty. The context decides which meaning fits. Debt is usually a noun for money that a person or organisation owes: “The business repaid its debt to the bank.” In “I owe you a debt of gratitude”, debt is figurative and means a strong feeling of obligation because someone has helped you. Forgiveness is a noun meaning the act of pardoning someone for a mistake or offence: “Her forgiveness helped them rebuild their friendship.” Pardon is a suitable near-synonym in this context. A synonym must fit the sentence; words from the same general topic are not automatically interchangeable.

Rail also has different meanings and word classes. As a verb, rail (usually followed by at or against) means complain angrily: “The residents railed against the unfair decision.” Railed is its past form. As a noun, a rail can be a fixed bar that people hold for support: “She held the rail as she walked down the stairs.” Rail can also mean one of the metal bars that form a railway track: “Workers inspected a damaged rail on the railway track.” In everyday writing, railway track or rail line is often clearer for the whole track. The sentence around the word tells you which meaning is intended.

The original Week 1 evaluation does not supply a passage, answer key or marks for its three rail items. Its sentence “The woman railed profusely when talking” is not a good model for the verb: rail is normally used with at or against when it means complain angrily, and profusely does not express the meaning of the verb. “I have walked down the rail on the stair case” is also unclear; a person may hold or walk beside a handrail, not normally walk down the bar itself. The vehicle sentence needs to identify a railway track or crossing. This lesson therefore uses new, clearly contextualised examples and questions. It does not claim to reconstruct the missing passage or an official source key.

Use a dictionary carefully. Check the headword, part of speech, pronunciation, numbered sense, example sentence and common grammatical pattern. For a verb such as rail, notice whether it needs a preposition (rail against a decision). For a noun such as rail, read the example to distinguish a support bar from a railway track. When a source gloss conflicts with a reliable dictionary, record the discrepancy and teach a corrected, labelled explanation without silently changing the source document.

practice.question: Read the sentences: (a) “That man is my father.” (b) “Security officers man the gate.” For each occurrence, state the part of speech and its meaning.
practice.answer: (a) Noun: an adult male person. (b) Verb: to staff the gate and be present to operate or control it.

marking.criterion: (a) gives the adult male person sense

practice.question: A learner says that “man the gate” means “guide the gate” and “man the office” always means “manage the organisation”. Correct both explanations using a dictionary-based meaning.
practice.answer: To man a gate is to staff the post and be present to operate or control it. To man an office is to staff or work at the office; it does not by itself mean to manage the whole organisation. Guide means show someone the way; manage means direct or control an organisation or activity.

marking.criterion: corrects man the gate to staff/operate the post
corrects man the office to staff/work there

practice.question: Give a suitable synonym for the bracketed word in each sentence. (a) I [appreciate] the help you gave me. (b) The business repaid its [debt] to the bank. (c) Her [forgiveness] helped them rebuild their friendship.
practice.answer: (a) value / am grateful for. (b) money owed / liability. (c) pardon / act of pardoning. The synonym must fit the meaning in the sentence.

practice.question: Give the meaning of the bracketed word in each original sentence. (a) The residents [railed] against the unfair decision. (b) She held the [rail] as she walked down the stairs. (c) Workers inspected a damaged [rail] on the railway track.
practice.answer: (a) complained angrily / protested. (b) a fixed bar used for support / a handrail. (c) one of the metal bars forming a railway track.

practice.question: Explain why each source-style sentence needs clearer wording, then rewrite it naturally: (a) “The woman railed profusely when talking.” (b) “I have walked down the rail on the stair case.” (c) “The rail is risky for vehicles to cross.”
practice.answer: (a) Rail meaning complain angrily normally takes at/against; profusely does not express that sense. Rewrite: “The woman railed against the unfair decision.” (b) A person holds or walks beside a handrail, not down the bar. Rewrite: “I held the handrail as I walked down the staircase.” (c) Identify the railway crossing/track. Rewrite: “Road vehicles must stop before crossing the railway track.”

marking.criterion: (a) explains collocation and supplies natural rewrite
(b) explains the physical meaning and supplies natural rewrite
(c) clarifies the railway meaning and supplies natural rewrite

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Original revision practice: selected 2nd Term English skills
objectives: Revise base words, prefixes and suffixes using meaningful word analysis.
Read an original passage to retrieve details, make a supported inference, scan for a fact and summarise the main idea.
Choose context-appropriate synonyms and distinguish gradable from complementary opposites.
Select adverbs and verb tenses that fit meaning and time relationships.
Distinguish narrative, descriptive, expository and argumentative purposes and write a relevant topic sentence.
lessons.body:
This original revision activity reviews only the SS1 English skills already taught in the current 2nd Term supplementary lessons: affixes and word formation; reading for details, inference, scanning and summary; synonyms, antonyms and contextual choice; adverbs and tense; and the purposes and organisation of common essay types. It is a practice revision activity, not a claim to reproduce an unavailable textbook paper or an official end-of-term examination. It does not cover 2nd Term topics that have not yet been taught in the available lessons.

1. Affixes and word formation. A base is the central form to which an affix is added. A prefix comes before the base (re- + write = rewrite); a suffix follows it (kind + -ness = kindness). Check that the added letters form a meaningful affix in the word; an accidental sequence of letters is not enough. When analysing a word, identify the base and the affix separately.

2. Reading. Read the whole passage once to understand its subject and main idea. Skimming means reading quickly for the general sense. Scanning means searching for a particular fact, name, date or figure. An inference is a conclusion supported by clues in the passage, not a guess. A summary keeps the main points, uses concise wording and adds no information that the passage does not contain.

3. Meaning in context. A synonym is a word with a similar meaning, but it must fit the sentence and preserve the intended sense. An antonym expresses an opposite. Gradable opposites allow degrees (for example, warm/cool); complementary opposites describe alternatives where one excludes the other in the relevant sense (for example, present/absent). Read the full sentence before choosing either.

4. Adverbs and tense. Adverbs can modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs. Choose a tense that matches the time relationship: the simple present can express a habit; the present continuous an activity happening now; the simple past a finished past event; the present perfect a past event connected with the present; and the past perfect an event earlier than another past event. Do not rely on a single time word without checking the whole sentence.

5. Essay types. A narrative tells events, usually in a sequence. A descriptive essay creates a clear picture of a person, place, object or experience. An expository essay explains a topic. An argumentative essay presents a position and supports it with relevant reasons and evidence. A useful paragraph has a clear main idea, supporting details and a logical link to the next point.

practice.question: Analyse the following words by identifying the base and the affix. State whether the affix is a prefix or suffix: (a) rewrite (b) kindness (c) careless (d) preview (e) joyful.
practice.answer: (a) re- + write: base write, prefix re-. (b) kind + -ness: base kind, suffix -ness. (c) care + -less: base care, suffix -less. (d) pre- + view: base view, prefix pre-. (e) joy + -ful: base joy, suffix -ful.

marking.criterion: Correct base and prefix in rewrite
Correct base and suffix in kindness
Correct base and suffix in careless
Correct base and prefix in preview
Correct base and suffix in joyful

practice.question: Read the original passage and answer the questions that follow. “Last term, the students started a small garden behind the science block. At first, only eight learners volunteered. They collected used containers, filled them with soil and planted spinach and tomatoes. The science teacher showed them how to water the plants without wasting water. By the sixth week, more students had joined because they could see fresh leaves growing. The group now plans to share some vegetables with the school kitchen and keep a record of each harvest.” (a) Where was the garden started? (b) How many learners volunteered at first? (c) What can you infer about why more students joined? (d) Which reading skill would help you quickly find the number of initial volunteers? (e) Write one sentence summarising the passage.
practice.answer: (a) Behind the science block. (b) Eight learners. (c) They joined because visible growth showed that the project was succeeding or interesting. (d) Scanning. (e) Sample: Students began a small school garden, learned to care for it and plan to share and record its harvest. Accept another concise summary that includes the main idea and does not add unsupported facts.

marking.criterion: Reasonable inference supported by visible plant growth
Accurate concise summary without invented detail

practice.question: (a) Give a context-appropriate synonym for “assist” in “The older pupils assist the new learners.” (b) Give a context-appropriate synonym for “silent” in “The room became silent during the announcement.” (c) Give an antonym of “generous”. (d) State whether “hot/cold” is a gradable or complementary pair. (e) State whether “alive/dead” is normally a gradable or complementary pair in its basic sense.
practice.answer: (a) help. (b) quiet. (c) selfish / mean / ungenerous. (d) Gradable: something can be warm, cool or lukewarm between the extremes. (e) Complementary in the basic sense used here: one is not both alive and dead at the same time.

marking.criterion: Assist = help or equivalent fitting the sentence
Silent = quiet or equivalent fitting the sentence
Identifies alive/dead as complementary in the stated basic sense

practice.question: Choose the correct form or word and give a brief reason: (a) Musa (walks / is walking) to school every day. (b) The children (play / are playing) in the field now. (c) We (visited / have visited) the museum yesterday. (d) By the time the bell rang, the lesson (started / had started). (e) She worked (hard / hardly) to complete the assignment.
practice.answer: (a) walks — habitual action. (b) are playing — action happening now. (c) visited — yesterday is a finished past time. (d) had started — the lesson began before the bell rang. (e) hard — means with effort; hardly means almost not.

marking.criterion: are playing with suitable current-action reason
hard, not hardly, with correct distinction

practice.question: (a) Match each purpose to its essay type: telling how an event happened; explaining how clean water is treated; describing a busy market; arguing that every school should have a reading club. (b) Write a suitable topic sentence for a paragraph supporting the view that every school should have a reading club.
practice.answer: (a) Telling how an event happened — narrative; explaining water treatment — expository; describing a busy market — descriptive; arguing for a reading club — argumentative. (b) Sample: “Every school should have a reading club because it helps learners develop confidence and a regular reading habit.” Accept another clear topic sentence that states a supporting reason.

marking.criterion: Clear relevant topic sentence stating a supportable reason

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Using a dictionary: word class, pronunciation, stress and collocation
objectives: Identify the word class and relevant sense of a dictionary headword.
Read IPA symbols including schwa, the length mark and primary and secondary stress marks.
Use dictionary pronunciation and stress information for ten advanced vocabulary items in a stated British English reference variety.
Explain meanings and use the ten words in grammatical patterns and collocations.
Write original sentences that demonstrate accurate word use.
lessons.body:
A dictionary is more than a list of meanings. A useful entry can show the headword, part of speech, pronunciation, stress, one or more senses, grammatical patterns and examples of how the word combines with other words. Read the entry for the exact sense you need; a word may have more than one meaning or grammatical use.

**A corrected model entry: abuse**

- **Noun:** /əˈbjuːs/ — harmful or improper treatment; the misuse of something. Common combinations include *physical abuse*, *verbal abuse* and *drug abuse*.
- **Verb:** /əˈbjuːz/ — to use something wrongly or treat a person or animal in a harmful way. Common combinations include *abuse power*, *abuse a privilege* and *abuse a person*.
- **Pronunciation:** /ə/ is the IPA schwa, not a Cyrillic character. /uː/ contains the IPA length mark /ː/. The stress mark /ˈ/ comes immediately before the stressed syllable: ə-ˈbjuːs and ə-ˈbjuːz. The noun and verb differ in their final consonant: /s/ in the noun and /z/ in the verb.
- **Word class:** the noun names the harmful treatment or misuse; the verb describes the action.

The ten original dictionary-study words below use a British English reference pronunciation. IPA is a guide to a reference accent, not a claim that every English accent sounds identical. In each transcription, /ˈ/ marks primary stress and /ˌ/ marks secondary stress. The long-vowel symbol /ː/ is part of the IPA transcription; it is not an ordinary colon.

| Word | Class | British English IPA | Meaning and use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **rapport** | noun | /ræˈpɔː/ | a friendly, understanding relationship; e.g. build rapport with; establish rapport between. |
| **acquaint** | verb | /əˈkweɪnt/ | make someone familiar with a fact, person or situation; e.g. acquaint someone with something; become acquainted with. |
| **defer** | verb | /dɪˈfɜː/ | postpone something; also yield respectfully to another person's judgement; e.g. defer a decision; defer to an expert. |
| **solicit** | verb | /səˈlɪsɪt/ | ask for or try to obtain something, often formally; e.g. solicit advice, donations or a response. |
| **acquiesce** | verb | /ˌæk.wiˈes/ | accept or agree without protest, even if it is not one's first choice; e.g. acquiesce in a decision; acquiesce to a demand. |
| **cohere** | verb | /kəʊˈhɪə/ | form a united, logical or consistent whole; stick together; e.g. ideas cohere; a coherent argument. |
| **comply** | verb | /kəmˈplaɪ/ | act according to a rule, request or instruction; e.g. comply with a rule or safety requirement. |
| **concur** | verb | /kənˈkɜː/ | agree with an opinion or happen at the same time; e.g. concur with an opinion; concur in a decision. |
| **obsess** | verb | /əbˈses/ | occupy someone's thoughts continually or excessively; e.g. obsess about a result; be obsessed with a detail. |
| **concede** | verb | /kənˈsiːd/ | admit that something is true or yield something, often after disagreement; e.g. concede a point; concede defeat. |

**How to study an entry:** identify the headword and word class; read the pronunciation and locate the stress mark; select the sense that fits the sentence; note the grammatical pattern and common collocations; then write your own sentence. Do not copy a dictionary's example sentence as your own work. If a word has more than one sense, record the sense used in your sentence.

practice.answer: Both forms are shown as a noun and a verb respectively. Noun /əˈbjuːs/ ends in /s/; verb /əˈbjuːz/ ends in /z/. Both have stress on the second syllable.

practice.question: Choose the correct word and form: (a) The school will (defer / solicit) the trip until the roads are safe. (b) The group will (solicit / cohere) donations for the library. (c) All drivers must (comply / concur) with the safety rules.

practice.question: Complete each sentence with a suitable form of acquiesce, concur or concede: (a) After discussion, I ______ with your conclusion. (b) Although she disagreed, she decided to ______ in the arrangement without protest. (c) He finally had to ______ that the evidence was correct.

practice.question: Match each word to its meaning: (a) acquaint (b) cohere (c) obsess (d) rapport. Meanings: a friendly understanding relationship; to make familiar with; to form a logical whole; to occupy the mind excessively.
practice.answer: (a) to make familiar with; (b) to form a logical whole; (c) to occupy the mind excessively; (d) a friendly understanding relationship.

lessons.title: Commonly misspelt words: spelling patterns, word division and correction
objectives: Correct common spelling errors using word structure, reliable spelling cues and dictionary checking.
Explain useful spelling cues for eleven original parallel word pairs without presenting them as source quotations.
Correct all ten Week 1 evaluation words, including the two-word form bus stop.
Use corrected spellings accurately in meaningful sentences.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT LESSON — Commonly misspelt words
This is a newly authored parallel lesson. Its eleven-word study list is original practice, not a transcription of the unavailable textbook list. The ten evaluation words named in the school source are retained below as targets for correction.

A reliable way to improve spelling is to notice the word's meaningful parts, identify a spelling pattern where one genuinely applies, and check doubtful forms in a dictionary. Do not force one rule onto every word.

Eleven original study pairs, with a reason or useful spelling cue:
1. accomodation → accommodation: the standard spelling has double c and double m.
2. begining → beginning: begin takes -ing and doubles its final n (beginning).
3. goverment → government: the word is govern + -ment; keep the n before the suffix.
4. seperate → separate: remember the a in the middle syllable: sep-a-rate.
5. recieve → receive: receive is spelt with ei after c; spelling rules have exceptions, so check unfamiliar words.
6. definately → definitely: definitely comes from definite + -ly; the correct form has i, not a.
7. enviroment → environment: keep the full spelling environ- before -ment.
8. adress → address: address has double d and double s.
9. succesful → successful: successful is formed from success + -ful; retain the double c and double s in success.
10. occassion → occasion: occasion has double c but one s.
11. grammer → grammar: grammar has double m and ends in -ar.

The Week 1 evaluation contains ten further targets. The accepted corrections are: grammer → grammar; guidiance → guidance; fourty → forty; intrest → interest; grieivous → grievous; mispel → misspell; bustop → bus stop; noticable → noticeable; ocasion → occasion; occured → occurred. The owner has confirmed that bustop is intended as the two-word expression bus stop.

Useful checks:
- Guidance is formed from guide + -ance; the final e is not retained before this suffix.
- Forty is the standard spelling; it does not retain the u in four.
- Grievous is spelt g-r-i-e-v-o-u-s. Do not insert an extra i.
- Misspell contains the prefix mis- and the complete base spell, including its double l.
- Bus stop is a two-word noun compound: bus + stop.
- Noticeable retains the e in notice to preserve the soft c sound.
- Occurred has double c and double r.
- Interest is spelt i-n-t-e-r-e-s-t; learn the full form rather than guessing from pronunciation.

When proofreading, read the whole sentence, check the word's meaning and grammatical form, and consult a dictionary if uncertain.

practice.answer: accommodation; beginning; government; separate; receive; definitely; environment; address; successful; occasion; grammar.

practice.answer: grammar; guidance; forty; interest; grievous; misspell; bus stop; noticeable; occasion; occurred.

practice.question: Write five meaningful sentences, each using one of these words correctly: accommodation, guidance, grievous, noticeable and occurred.
practice.answer: Accept any five grammatically correct sentences that use the selected words with their correct meanings and spelling.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Contextual word meanings: an original reading passage and keyed comprehension
objectives: Use surrounding sentences and grammatical context to infer word meanings.
Explain the contextual use of sex as an administrative category in the original passage.
Explain leave in the phrase leave a lasting impression as make or produce an effect.
Answer comprehension and reading-assignment questions with evidence from an original passage.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT READING ACTIVITY — Contextual meanings
This passage and its questions are original. They are a parallel activity for reading to understand words in context; they do not reproduce Effective English Unit 8 page 133 or Unit 10 page 162.

Comprehension: Contextual use of words
Content: Reading
Contextual usage of words

Passage — A fairer discussion
At the beginning of the school year, the debate club noticed that a few confident members answered nearly every question while some quieter learners rarely spoke. The club secretary suggested that the teacher should keep a simple record of attendance and participation. The school's approved registration form also asked for each learner's sex as an administrative category. The teacher explained that a form entry is only the information requested for that record; it does not tell anyone what a learner believes or how confidently that learner can speak.

The chairperson introduced a new routine. Each member was invited to make one contribution before anyone spoke for a second time. Members who preferred to think before speaking could write one idea on a card. The chairperson then invited them to explain their ideas in their own words.

After four meetings, more learners had contributed. The club still had disagreements, but members listened more carefully and gave reasons for their views. The teacher said that the new routine could leave a lasting impression on the group because it showed that every member's contribution mattered. The club decided to keep the routine and review it at the end of the term.

How to work out meaning from context:
1. Read the whole sentence and the sentence before or after it.
2. Identify the word's grammatical job.
3. Suggest a meaning that fits the situation.
4. Replace the word with your suggested meaning and check that the sentence still makes sense.
5. Do not assume that a word has only one meaning in every context.

In this passage, sex is the administrative category requested by the registration form. The phrase leave a lasting impression means make or produce a lasting effect on someone's memory or feelings; it does not mean depart from a place. The source note also mentions another dictionary sense of sex. This original equivalent does not teach that additional sense pending the teacher's direction; it does not claim to reconstruct the missing textbook passage.

For a reading assignment, answer the questions using evidence from the passage. A good answer is relevant, clear and no longer than the question requires. A summary states the central point without adding personal opinions or details not found in the passage.

practice.question: What problem did the debate club notice at the beginning of the year?
practice.answer: A few confident members answered nearly every question while quieter learners rarely spoke.

practice.question: State two changes the chairperson introduced.
practice.answer: Each member was invited to contribute once before anyone spoke again; members could write an idea on a card before explaining it.

marking.criterion: One contribution before a second turn
Writing an idea on a card before speaking

practice.question: What does sex refer to in the passage, and what does leave mean in the phrase leave a lasting impression?
practice.answer: Sex is the administrative category requested by the registration form. Leave means make or produce in the phrase leave a lasting impression.

marking.criterion: Contextual meaning of sex in the form
Leave = make or produce an effect

practice.question: Why did the teacher say the form entry does not tell anyone what a learner believes or how confidently the learner can speak?
practice.answer: Because the form records one administrative category only; it does not describe a person's opinions or speaking confidence.

marking.criterion: Recognises the limited purpose of the form
Distinguishes the form entry from beliefs or confidence

practice.question: Write one sentence summarising the passage.
practice.answer: Sample: The debate club introduced a fairer speaking routine so that more learners could contribute and be heard. Accept another accurate sentence that captures the central idea without adding unsupported information.

marking.criterion: Captures the aim of including more voices
Concise and faithful to the passage

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Reading for the main point: Beauty (original passage and keyed comprehension)
objectives: Identify the main point of a complete passage.
Distinguish a main point from a supporting detail and a topic label.
Support a proposed main point with relevant details from the passage.
Write a concise summary that preserves the central idea.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT PASSAGE — Beauty
This passage is newly authored for SS1 English 3rd Term Week 2. It is not a reproduction of a prescribed textbook passage.

Comprehension: Reading for the main point
Passage — Beauty

People often think that beauty is only what the eyes notice first: bright colours, neat buildings or attractive clothes. These things can be pleasing, but they do not tell the whole story. A place can become beautiful because people care for it and make it welcoming to others.

At the edge of a town, an old public garden had become untidy. Plastic wrappers lay near the footpath, the benches were dusty, and the flower beds were almost empty. Some residents said that the garden was no longer worth visiting. A group of students and neighbours decided to improve it instead of complaining about it.

They began by collecting litter and sorting materials that could be reused. A carpenter repaired two benches, while younger children watered the plants. The students planted flowers along the path and placed simple signs asking visitors to keep the garden clean. They did not finish everything in one day, but they returned each Saturday.

After several weeks, families began using the garden again. The flowers added colour, yet visitors also noticed the clean paths, repaired seats and friendly greetings. The garden's beauty came not only from its appearance but also from the patience and cooperation that had restored it.

The main point is the central idea the writer wants the reader to understand. It is broader than one detail and more precise than a one-word topic. Supporting details explain, illustrate or provide evidence for the main point.

To find the main point:
1. Read the whole passage, not only the first sentence.
2. Ask what idea connects the paragraphs.
3. Separate the central idea from examples, names and minor facts.
4. Check that the proposed main point is supported by more than one part of the passage.
5. State it in one clear sentence.

For this passage, the topic is beauty. The main point is that beauty is not only outward appearance; care, patience and cooperation can also make a place beautiful. The flowers, repaired benches and clean paths are supporting details. A statement about only the flowers would be too narrow.

When answering, give the central idea in your own words and use details from the passage to support it. Do not add claims about the writer's intentions that the passage does not support.

practice.question: State the main point of the passage in one clear sentence.
practice.answer: Beauty is not only outward appearance; care, patience and cooperation can also make a place beautiful.

marking.criterion: Recognises that beauty is more than outward appearance
Includes care, patience, cooperation or positive action as part of beauty

practice.question: Give two actions the students and neighbours took to improve the garden.
practice.answer: They collected litter, sorted reusable materials, repaired benches, watered plants, planted flowers or placed signs. Any two supported actions.

marking.criterion: First accurate action from the passage
Second accurate action from the passage

practice.question: Why did families begin using the garden again?
practice.answer: It had become cleaner, more welcoming and more attractive, with repaired benches, flowers and friendly greetings.

marking.criterion: Explains how the improvements made it welcoming or attractive

practice.question: Why is “The flowers added colour” a supporting detail rather than the main point?
practice.answer: It describes one example of the garden's improvement, while the main point connects the whole passage: beauty also comes from care and cooperation.

marking.criterion: Identifies the sentence as one specific detail
Contrasts it with the broader central idea

practice.question: Write a one-sentence summary of the passage.
practice.answer: Sample: Students and neighbours restored an untidy garden, showing that beauty grows from both appearance and the care people give a place. Accept another concise and accurate summary.

marking.criterion: Includes the restoration or community effort
Captures the central message without unsupported detail

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Summary writing: question-and-answer summaries, precis and original reading practice
objectives: Distinguish a question-and-answer summary from a precis.
Apply seven practical habits for concise, accurate summary writing.
Summarise an original passage in a stated word limit without adding unsupported ideas.
Answer an original reading assignment using evidence from the passage.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT LESSON — Summary writing
This lesson is original. Its passage, reading assignment, questions and marking guide are not taken from Effective English Book 1 pages 212–215 or Countdown English pages 111–112.

Two approaches to summary:
1. Question-and-answer summary: answer each question separately, using only the information needed for that question. Keep each answer clear and concise. Use your own words where possible, but do not change the meaning.
2. Precis: write one shorter, connected passage that preserves the central ideas and their logical order. A precis is not a list of answers; it is a compact version of the whole passage.

The source scheme recommends the question-and-answer approach in its WAEC preparation context. That is recorded as the scheme's recommendation, not asserted here as a universal or current examination-board rule. Follow the instructions and current marking guidance for the examination you are preparing for.

Seven useful summary habits:
1. Read the passage more than once: first for the general meaning, then to locate the points needed.
2. Identify the main points and the links between them.
3. Be concise. Remove examples and repetition unless they are essential to the answer.
4. Use your own words where you can do so accurately; do not replace a precise term with a misleading synonym.
5. Do not add opinions, explanations or facts that the passage does not contain.
6. Write clear, complete and grammatical sentences. Number answers only when the question or teacher asks you to do so.
7. Check that each answer is relevant, unambiguous and within the stated word or sentence limit.

Do not treat an unsupported statement about penalties or zero marks as an official examination rule. Only a current, authorised examination guide can establish a particular board's marking policy.

Original passage — The school rainwater project
During the dry season, the school garden often dried out because water was difficult to carry from the distant tap. The science club proposed collecting rainwater from the classroom roof. With permission, learners cleaned the gutters, placed a covered storage tank beside the garden and fitted a simple filter to keep leaves out. The caretaker checked the tank each week, while club members used small watering cans to share the stored water among the plants. They recorded how much water they used and kept the tank covered to prevent dirt and mosquitoes from entering. The project did not replace the school's normal water supply, but it reduced the need to carry water during short dry periods. The head teacher asked other classes to suggest ways of saving water.

Original reading assignment — The repair club
At the end of each month, the school repair club checks desks, shelves and classroom doors. Learners report damage to the teacher rather than trying to repair electrical equipment themselves. The teacher assigns safe jobs, such as tightening loose screws under supervision, sorting books and labelling shelves. The club records completed work and asks for help with repairs that require a trained adult. Because small problems are reported early, classrooms remain safer and equipment lasts longer.

When summarising, preserve the central message, not every small detail. A summary must be shorter than the original and must not introduce an idea simply because it seems sensible.

practice.question: Name the two approaches to summary writing and explain one difference between them.
practice.answer: The question-and-answer approach gives separate concise answers to specific questions. A precis gives one connected, shortened version of the whole passage while preserving its main ideas and order.

marking.criterion: Explains that answers are given separately
Explains that a precis is a connected shortened version of the whole passage

practice.question: State seven useful habits for writing a clear summary.
practice.answer: Read more than once; identify main points and links; be concise; use accurate own words; omit personal opinion and unsupported additions; write clear grammatical sentences and number only when asked; check relevance, clarity and the required limit.

marking.criterion: Read the passage more than once
Be concise and remove unnecessary detail
Write clearly and number only when instructed
Check relevance, clarity and the stated limit

practice.question: Summarise The school rainwater project in no more than 45 words.
practice.answer: The science club collected rainwater from the classroom roof in a covered tank. Learners filtered and shared the water carefully, recorded its use and kept the tank clean. The project helped the garden during dry periods and encouraged the school to consider further water-saving ideas.

marking.criterion: Includes rainwater collection from the roof
Explains the benefit to the garden or school

practice.question: Answer the original reading assignment: (a) What does the club inspect? (b) Why do learners report electrical damage to the teacher? (c) Give one safe job. (d) What is one result of reporting small problems early? (e) State the main idea in one sentence.
practice.answer: (a) Desks, shelves and classroom doors. (b) Electrical repairs require a trained adult and may be unsafe for learners. (c) Tightening loose screws under supervision, sorting books or labelling shelves. (d) Classrooms remain safer and equipment lasts longer. (e) The repair club helps keep the school safe by reporting and addressing small maintenance problems.

marking.criterion: Explains why electrical repairs go to an adult

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Advertising vocabulary: six reviewed terms and original reading practice
objectives: Explain advertisement, advertising, target audience, publicity, market and branding.
Distinguish an individual advertisement from the wider activity of advertising.
Distinguish publicity from a paid advertisement and identify a target audience.
Apply the six terms in original gap-fill and reading-comprehension practice.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT LESSON — Advertising vocabulary
The definitions below are original paraphrases checked against learner-dictionary and business-dictionary usage. The passage and exercises are original.

Six useful terms:
1. Advertisement: a particular message, picture, recording or notice intended to inform people about something or persuade them to consider a product, service, job or event.
2. Advertising: the organised activity of preparing and placing promotional messages so that an intended group notices a product, service or idea. An advertisement is one message; advertising is the wider activity.
3. Target (target audience): the particular group of people a campaign is designed to reach. The target audience should be identified before choosing the message and medium.
4. Publicity: public attention or information about a person, organisation, product or event. Publicity may arise from news coverage or public discussion; it is not necessarily a paid advertisement controlled by the organisation.
5. Market: the group of actual or potential buyers for a product or service, together with the conditions and channels through which buyers and sellers interact. It does not mean only the buyers.
6. Branding: the work of creating a recognisable identity for a product, service or organisation through a name, design, symbol, style and consistent associations.

Do not use advertisement and advertising as if they always name the same thing. Do not define publicity only as paid advertising: news coverage may create publicity without being a paid advertisement. A target audience is more precise than simply saying “the target”. A market includes more than a list of customers.

Original reading assignment — Reading Week campaign
During Reading Week, the school planned a campaign to encourage learners to borrow books. The librarian asked the art club to design a poster, while the debate club prepared a short announcement for assembly. The poster named the library hours and showed a drawing of students reading. A local radio station later mentioned the event after receiving a news release; the school did not pay for that report. The campaign was aimed mainly at SS1 learners who had not yet borrowed a book. The librarian recorded how many new borrowers joined during the week.

When studying an advert, ask: What is being promoted? Who is the intended audience? What message is being given? Which medium carries it? Is the claim clear and fair?

practice.question: Match each term to its meaning: advertisement; advertising; target audience; publicity; market; branding.
practice.answer: Advertisement — one promotional message. Advertising — the organised activity of creating and placing promotional messages. Target audience — the group the campaign is designed to reach. Publicity — public attention or information about something. Market — actual and potential buyers and the conditions/channels of exchange. Branding — creating a recognisable identity.

practice.question: Choose the best word for each gap from the options in brackets. (a) A large roadside board displaying a message is a (billboard / newsletter / end-user). (b) The person or organisation responsible for placing an advert is the (advertiser / agent / end-user). (c) Short paid messages between television programmes are (commercials / announcements / news casting). (d) A person who buys or uses a product is a (consumer / advertising agency / public relations unit). (e) A reduction from the usual price is a (gift / dash / discount).
practice.answer: (a) billboard. (b) advertiser. (c) commercials. (d) consumer. (e) discount.

practice.question: Use the Reading Week campaign passage. (a) Identify its target audience. (b) Name two communication channels used by the school. (c) Which event created publicity rather than a paid school advertisement? (d) State the campaign's purpose.
practice.answer: (a) SS1 learners who had not yet borrowed a book. (b) The poster and the assembly announcement; the radio report is also a channel of publicity. (c) The local radio station's unpaid report after receiving the news release. (d) To encourage learners to borrow books.

marking.criterion: Names the assembly announcement or radio report
Distinguishes the unpaid radio report as publicity
States the purpose of encouraging book borrowing

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Adjuncts: forms, six classroom categories and original keyed practice
objectives: Define an adjunct as an optional clause element that adds circumstantial information.
Recognise adjuncts realised by adverbs, phrases and clauses.
Classify adjuncts by manner, time, place, degree, frequency and direction.
Write and identify original sentences containing the six classroom categories.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT LESSON — Adjuncts
An adjunct is an optional element of a clause that adds information about the circumstances of an event or situation. It is not simply “a type of adverb”. An adjunct may be realised by an adverb (carefully), a prepositional phrase (after lunch), a noun phrase (next week) or a clause (because the rain stopped). An adjunct can often be removed while the basic clause remains grammatical, although the meaning becomes less specific. Do not confuse an optional adjunct with a complement required to complete a verb's meaning.

Six classroom categories:
1. Manner — how? Example: The class worked carefully.
2. Time — when or for how long? Example: We met after lunch.
3. Place — where? Example: The pupils waited in the hall.
4. Degree — to what extent? Example: The team nearly finished the task.
5. Frequency — how often? Example: She practises every evening.
6. Direction — where to or from? Example: The children ran towards the gate.

These are useful introductory meaning groups, not a claim that all grammar books use exactly the same six-part list. Some expressions can fit more than one group depending on their use. For example, again can refer to another time and can also suggest repetition or frequency. Read the whole sentence and ask what information the expression contributes.

Worked examples:
- The pupils were taught well. Adjunct: well (manner; how?).
- The meeting ended happily. Adjunct: happily (manner; how?).
- We will commence now. Adjunct: now (time; when?).
- I will see you later. Adjunct: later (time; when?).
- She sometimes forgets her notebook. Adjunct: sometimes (frequency; how often?).
- The bus continued towards the station. Adjunct: towards the station (direction; where to?).

Original reading assignment — A day at the science fair
At dawn, the team walked slowly across the field. They waited near the gate for ten minutes. Later, they carried the boxes inside. The teacher almost forgot to bring the list, but she checked it carefully. At the end, the pupils moved towards the hall.

To analyse an adjunct, identify the expression, decide whether it is a word, phrase or clause, and ask which circumstance it adds. The question it answers is a helpful clue, not a substitute for reading the sentence.

practice.question: In “The pupils worked carefully in the laboratory after lunch”, identify three adjuncts and state the form of each.
practice.answer: carefully — adverb; in the laboratory — prepositional phrase; after lunch — prepositional phrase.

marking.criterion: States that carefully is an adverb
States that in the laboratory is a prepositional phrase
States that after lunch is a prepositional phrase

practice.question: Name the category of each adjunct: (a) slowly (b) yesterday (c) outside the classroom (d) nearly (e) twice a week (f) towards the bridge.
practice.answer: (a) manner; (b) time; (c) place; (d) degree; (e) frequency; (f) direction.

practice.question: Write six original sentences, one containing an adjunct of each category: manner, time, place, degree, frequency and direction. Put the adjunct in square brackets and label its category.
practice.answer: Examples: (1) The choir sang [beautifully] (manner). (2) We arrived [before noon] (time). (3) The pupils waited [in the library] (place). (4) She [almost] dropped the cup (degree). (5) He visits [every Saturday] (frequency). (6) The runners moved [towards the finish line] (direction). Accept other accurate sentences.

marking.criterion: Manner sentence with correctly identified adjunct
Time sentence with correctly identified adjunct
Place sentence with correctly identified adjunct
Degree sentence with correctly identified adjunct
Frequency sentence with correctly identified adjunct
Direction sentence with correctly identified adjunct

practice.question: From the A day at the science fair passage, identify six adjuncts and state their categories.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The narrative essay: features, worked plan, model and marked practice
objectives: Explain the purpose and basic structure of a narrative essay.
Identify setting, characters, connected events, problem, turning point and outcome.
Prepare a six-point plan for My Most Interesting Journey.
Write a coherent narrative using appropriate tense, viewpoint, paragraphing and relevant detail.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT LESSON — The narrative essay
A narrative essay tells a connected account of real or imagined events. It usually has a setting, characters, a situation or problem, a sequence of events, a turning point and an outcome. The writer chooses a point of view and keeps it consistent.

Useful features:
- Give the essay a clear title. A title is normally capitalised according to the school's chosen style.
- Establish the setting and the people involved.
- Arrange events in a logical order. Time expressions and paragraph links help the reader follow the story.
- Use a tense that suits the chosen narration. The past tense is common when recounting completed events, but a writer may use the present tense deliberately; consistency matters more than treating past tense as an unbreakable rule.
- Use specific verbs, sensory details and occasional dialogue to make events vivid.
- Develop paragraphs around stages of the story. Include a problem or interesting event, a turning point and a believable outcome.
- Figures of speech and proverbs may enrich a story, but they are choices, not compulsory ingredients in every narrative.
- End by showing what happened and, where appropriate, what the narrator learnt.

Worked plan — My Most Interesting Journey
1. Preparation: I packed water, a notebook and a small camera the night before.
2. Start: My aunt and I left early by bus to visit my cousin.
3. Feelings and sights: I felt excited and nervous as farms, hills and villages passed the window.
4. Interesting part: Heavy rain stopped the bus near a swollen stream. Local residents showed the driver a safe route. The water roared like a restless animal (simile).
5. Duration and arrival: The journey took about four hours; we arrived safely before evening.
6. Conclusion and lesson: I learnt to be patient, prepare carefully and appreciate people who help travellers.

Model narrative — My Most Interesting Journey
I had packed my bag the night before, but I still woke before sunrise to check it. My aunt was taking me by bus to visit my cousin in a town I had never seen. I was excited, although the long journey made me a little nervous.

At first, the road was smooth. I watched farms, hills and small markets pass the window. Near midday, dark clouds gathered and rain struck the roof. The driver slowed down when we reached a swollen stream. The water roared like a restless animal, and everyone became quiet.

The driver did not rush. He spoke with two residents who knew the area, then followed their directions along a safer road. We stopped briefly to let another vehicle pass before continuing. I was relieved when the bus reached the main road again.

We arrived at my cousin's town before evening. The journey had taken about four hours, but I remembered the kindness of the residents more than the delay. It was my most interesting journey because it taught me that patience, preparation and help from others can turn a difficult experience into a valuable lesson.

Original reading assignment — The missing notebook
When the bell rang, Tola discovered that her science notebook was missing. She searched her desk and asked her classmates whether anyone had seen it. Her friend Musa remembered that Tola had carried the notebook to the garden during the previous lesson. They returned to the garden and found it beneath a bench, protected from the rain by a plastic folder. Tola thanked Musa and promised to keep her books in her bag after class.

A narrative plan is not the essay itself. Develop each point into a connected paragraph, choose details that move the story forward, and make the ending follow naturally from the events.

practice.question: State five useful features of a narrative essay.
practice.answer: A suitable title; setting and characters; connected events in a logical order; a consistent point of view and tense; a problem or interesting event with a turning point and outcome; vivid details or dialogue where useful. Any five.

practice.question: Prepare a six-point outline for My Most Interesting Journey using the worked plan as a guide.
practice.answer: Preparation; departure; feelings and sights; the most interesting event; duration and arrival; conclusion and lesson learnt.

practice.question: Write a narrative essay on “A journey I will always remember”. Organise it into paragraphs and include a setting, people, connected events, an interesting or difficult incident, an outcome and a suitable ending.
practice.answer: Assess the learner's own original narrative using the rubric: relevance and development of events (4); logical sequence and paragraphing (4); setting, characters and vivid relevant detail (3); clear turning point and outcome (3); appropriate and consistent tense/point of view (3); grammar, spelling and punctuation (3). Total 20.

marking.criterion: Clear setting, characters and vivid details
Interesting incident, turning point and outcome
Appropriate consistent tense and point of view

practice.answer: (a) Tola. (b) Her science notebook is missing. (c) Musa remembers that she carried it to the garden; they return there. (d) They find the notebook beneath a bench in a plastic folder. (e) She should keep her books safely in her bag after class. Accept a sensible answer supported by the passage.

lessons.title: Week 2 weekend assessment: antonyms in context and clause examples
objectives: Choose context-appropriate antonyms for five target words or expressions.
Write examples of noun, adverbial and adjectival clauses.
Distinguish clause types by their function in a sentence.
Use model answers and a clear marking guide to review original practice.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT WEEKEND ASSESSMENT — Antonyms and clauses
This is an original practice set with a complete key. It repairs the missing options, unclear gaps and absent marking information in the source exercise without claiming to reproduce its original answers.

Part A — Antonyms in context
An antonym is a word or expression with an opposite meaning in the relevant context. Read the whole sentence before choosing an answer: the best opposite must fit both the meaning and the grammar.

Part B — Clause preview
A clause contains a verb and its associated elements. A noun clause functions like a noun phrase (for example, as a subject or object). An adverbial clause adds information such as time, reason or condition. An adjectival clause, also called a relative clause, describes a noun or noun phrase. The examples below are a short preview and practice; the broader clause topic is developed in the next teaching sequence.

Model distinctions:
- Noun clause: What she said surprised us. The clause What she said is the subject.
- Adverbial clause: We stayed inside because it was raining. The clause gives a reason.
- Adjectival/relative clause: The learner who won the prize thanked her teacher. The clause describes learner.

Original practice questions:
Use the five antonym items in Part A and the clause-writing task in Part B. Each response is marked separately.

practice.question: Choose a suitable opposite for the bold idea in each context. (a) The daring climber crossed the narrow bridge. (b) Instead of conforming to the unfair rule, the group decided to act independently. (c) The indigent family received help from its neighbours. (d) The teacher reprimanded the pupil for careless work. (e) The evidence convinced the panel of his innocence.
practice.answer: (a) timid/cautious. (b) rebel/resist/refuse to comply. (c) wealthy/affluent. (d) praised/commended. (e) convinced the panel of his guilt / believed to be guilty.

marking.criterion: Valid contextual opposite of convinced of his innocence

practice.question: Write five examples of noun clauses, three examples of adverbial clauses and three examples of adjectival (relative) clauses. Identify the function or meaning of each.
practice.answer: Noun clauses: (1) What she said surprised us (subject). (2) I know that he arrived (object). (3) Whoever finishes first may leave (subject). (4) She asked whether the bus had left (object). (5) My hope is that we succeed (subject complement). Adverbial clauses: (1) We stayed inside because it was raining (reason). (2) When the bell rang, the pupils lined up (time). (3) If you revise, you will improve (condition). Adjectival clauses: (1) The book that you lent me is useful. (2) The learner who won the prize thanked her teacher. (3) The house where my aunt lives is near the market. Each adjectival clause describes a noun.

marking.criterion: One correct noun clause with suitable function
Second correct noun clause with suitable function
Third correct noun clause with suitable function
Fourth correct noun clause with suitable function
Fifth correct noun clause with suitable function
One correct adverbial clause and meaning
Second correct adverbial clause and meaning
Third correct adverbial clause and meaning

Second correct adjectival/relative clause modifying a noun
Third correct adjectival/relative clause modifying a noun

practice.question: Identify each bracketed clause as a noun, adverbial or adjectival clause. (a) [What she said] surprised us. (b) We stayed home [because it rained]. (c) The girl [who won] smiled. (d) I wonder [whether he is ready]. (e) [When the bus arrived], we boarded. (f) The house [where I grew up] has been sold.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Comprehension and summary: original passages on fishing and leisure time
objectives: Read an original passage to retrieve facts and make supported inferences.
Answer comprehension questions using textual evidence.
Identify the central points of a passage and distinguish them from minor details.
Write concise summaries of original passages within the stated sentence limit.
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL EQUIVALENT LESSON — Comprehension and summary writing
These two passages and all questions are newly authored. They are parallel activities for the Week 3 reading and summary objectives; they do not reproduce Effective English pages 227–228 or 152–154, Countdown pages 220–224, or any other prescribed page.

Passage A — Fishing beside the river
In a riverside settlement, a group of young people joined an experienced fisher to learn how fishing was organised. They first checked the weather and examined the nets for holes. The fisher explained that different nets are suitable for different fish and that small fish should be returned to the water when local rules require it. The group also learnt to keep the riverbank clean and to avoid leaving plastic line where birds could become trapped.

Before sunrise, the learners helped carry the equipment to a safe landing place. They watched the fisher read the movement of the water and choose a suitable area. The group did not catch many fish that morning because the current was unusually strong. Instead of taking risks, they returned to the bank and discussed what they had observed. The fisher said that knowledge, patience and respect for the river were as important as the equipment.

Passage B — Leisure time
After completing their weekly schoolwork, three friends decided to use part of Saturday for a shared activity. One enjoyed drawing, another liked repairing old radios with an adult relative, and the third preferred playing football. They agreed to meet at the community centre, where each person could demonstrate a skill. The drawing student showed how to sketch a familiar street; the radio enthusiast explained why a loose connection can interrupt a signal; and the football player led a short exercise session.

The friends discovered that leisure time did not have to mean doing nothing. A chosen activity could provide rest, enjoyment and an opportunity to learn. They also agreed that recreation should leave enough time for homework, family responsibilities and sleep.

Reading for comprehension:
- Read the whole passage before answering.
- A factual answer should be supported by a sentence or detail in the passage.
- An inference is a reasonable conclusion supported by clues, not an invented event.
- A summary keeps the central points and removes minor examples.

Summary writing:
For a question-and-answer summary, answer each question separately and concisely. For a connected summary, combine the main points in your own words while preserving their meaning and order. Follow the exact instruction and word or sentence limit given by the teacher. Do not claim a universal examination-board rule unless an authorised current guide states it.

practice.question: From Passage A, state two checks the learners made before fishing.
practice.answer: They checked the weather and examined the nets for holes.

practice.question: Why did the group return to the bank instead of continuing to fish?
practice.answer: The river current was unusually strong, so continuing could have been unsafe.

practice.question: Give one inference about the fisher's attitude to the river, supported by the passage.
practice.answer: The fisher respects and cares for the river because the learners were taught to keep the bank clean, protect birds and follow local rules.

practice.question: Write a two-sentence summary of Passage A.
practice.answer: The learners joined an experienced fisher to learn safe, responsible fishing and care for the river. When the current became strong, they returned to shore and learnt that knowledge and patience matter as much as equipment.

marking.criterion: Includes care for river or local rules
Includes decision to return because of strong current
Concise and faithful to central meaning

practice.question: From Passage B, state the three activities the friends shared and give one benefit of leisure time mentioned in the passage.
practice.answer: Drawing, repairing old radios and playing football; a benefit is rest, enjoyment or an opportunity to learn.

practice.question: Write a one-sentence summary of Passage B.
practice.answer: Three friends used leisure time to share skills and enjoy useful activities while balancing recreation with schoolwork, family responsibilities and sleep.
