lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Argumentative essays: question types, planning and a worked justification
objectives: Explain the purpose and structure of an argumentative essay.
Distinguish for-or-against, balanced for-and-against, and justify question forms.
Plan and develop a reasoned argument with examples and a conclusion.
Write a coherent argumentative essay on patriotism and national development.
lessons.body:
An argumentative essay presents a clear position on an issue and supports it with reasons and relevant evidence. Its purpose is to persuade a reader to accept a position, while showing that the writer understands the issue. It is not simply a list of opinions: each major point needs an explanation or example.
Read the wording of the question before planning. Three common forms require different responses. (1) “Do you agree or disagree?” or “Write for or against …” asks you to choose one side and defend it. (2) “Discuss both sides” or “Give arguments for and against …” requires fair treatment of both positions before a reasoned conclusion. (3) “Justify the statement …” asks you to defend the stated position with reasons; you may acknowledge a limitation, but your main task is to justify the claim. Do not confuse a one-sided justification with a balanced discussion.
A reliable method is: define the issue in the introduction; state your position; plan three distinct reasons; support each reason with a relevant explanation or example; consider a reasonable opposing point where useful; and conclude by restating the position in fresh words. Keep paragraphs focused. Avoid insults, invented statistics and sweeping claims. A clear argument is stronger than an exaggerated one.
Worked plan for “Patriotism enhances the growth of a nation” (justify form). Position: responsible patriotism can support national development. Point 1: citizens who respect public property reduce waste and repair costs. Point 2: paying lawful taxes and demanding accountability can support public services. Point 3: citizens who cooperate across communities strengthen peace and productive work. Qualification: patriotism is not blind support for wrongdoing; responsible citizens may criticise unfair policies and seek lawful improvement. Conclusion: informed, responsible commitment to the common good can help a country develop.
Model paragraph: Responsible patriotism encourages citizens to protect shared resources. When people avoid damaging public facilities, schools, roads and health centres remain useful for longer and public funds can be directed to other needs. For example, a community that reports vandalism and helps keep its market clean creates a safer place for trade. Patriotism therefore becomes practical service rather than a slogan.
For a balanced “for and against” question, present the strongest reasonable case on each side, use linking expressions such as on the one hand, however and nevertheless, and reach a conclusion that follows from your discussion. For a “for or against” question, state your chosen side early and make every paragraph advance that case. For a “justify” question, explain why the stated claim is reasonable and support it with specific points.

practice.question: Classify each instruction: (a) Write for or against school uniforms. (b) Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of social media. (c) Justify the statement that reading improves learning.
practice.answer: (a) choose and defend one side; (b) balanced discussion of both sides; (c) defend the stated claim with reasons.

practice.question: Prepare a four-point plan for the topic “Patriotism enhances the growth of a nation”. Include a position and three distinct supporting reasons.
practice.answer: Accept a clear position and three relevant, distinct reasons such as protecting public property, contributing responsibly to public services, and cooperating across communities; each point should be explained.

practice.question: Write an argumentative essay of 180–220 words on “Patriotism enhances the growth of a nation”. Use an introduction, at least three supporting points and a conclusion. Acknowledge one reasonable qualification.
practice.answer: Award marks using the rubric. A strong response argues that responsible patriotism supports development through care for public assets, civic participation and social cooperation; it distinguishes patriotism from blind loyalty and concludes coherently.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 8 original revision: word stress, contextual meaning and debate
objectives: Identify primary word stress in five multisyllabic words.
Choose context-appropriate synonyms for five vocabulary items.
Prepare a respectful debate speech supporting or opposing a motion.
lessons.body:
This is an original revision set for Week 8. It does not reproduce or supply answers to the unavailable textbook tasks. Use the pronunciation guidance taught in class: a word's primary stress is the syllable spoken most strongly. In the broad British pronunciations below, the mark ˈ comes immediately before the primary-stressed syllable. Say each word aloud and compare the stressed syllable; do not guess from spelling alone.
Word-stress review: indoctrinate /ɪnˈdɒktrɪneɪt/ (second syllable); refinery /rɪˈfaɪnəri/ (second); phenomenal /fəˈnɒmɪnəl/ (second); consistency /kənˈsɪstənsi/ (second); acrobatic /ˌækrəˈbætɪk/ (third; the earlier ˌ marks secondary stress).
Meaning in context: momentarily means for a very short time; stealthily means secretly or quietly to avoid being noticed; squarely can mean directly or firmly; meticulous means extremely careful and attentive to detail; satisfied means pleased because a need or expectation has been met. Choose a synonym that fits the sentence, not merely one that shares a general topic.
A debate speech addresses a motion and tries to persuade an audience. State whether you support or oppose the motion, define any important term, give two or three clear reasons with examples, respond respectfully to an opposing point, and finish with a memorable conclusion. For the motion “Participation of women in government should be encouraged”, either side may be argued. A respectful opposing argument must address policy or implementation, not attack people because of sex or identity.

practice.question: For each word, state the syllable carrying primary stress: (a) indoctrinate; (b) refinery; (c) phenomenal; (d) consistency; (e) acrobatic.
practice.answer: (a) second; (b) second; (c) second; (d) second; (e) third.

practice.question: Choose the closest meaning in each context: (a) The lights went out momentarily. (briefly / permanently) (b) The thief moved stealthily. (secretly / noisily) (c) The criticism was aimed squarely at the manager. (directly / accidentally) (d) The meticulous editor checked every comma. (careless / very careful) (e) She was satisfied with the result. (pleased / confused).
practice.answer: (a) briefly; (b) secretly; (c) directly; (d) very careful; (e) pleased.

practice.question: Write a short debate speech of 120–150 words either supporting or opposing the motion: “Participation of women in government should be encouraged.” State your side, give at least two reasons, support them with examples and conclude respectfully.
practice.answer: Accept either side. The speech must address the motion, give at least two relevant reasons with explanation/examples, maintain respectful language and end with a clear conclusion.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Answering comprehension questions and contextual synonyms
objectives: Explain a practical sequence for answering comprehension questions.
Answer questions from an original passage using only stated or supported information.
Choose contextual synonyms while preserving grammatical form.
lessons.body:
Comprehension is the ability to understand a passage and respond accurately to what it says. Read the instructions first so that you know whether you must answer in your own words, choose a synonym, explain a phrase or give a short summary. Skim the passage once to identify its subject and general direction. Read the questions carefully; they tell you which details to locate. Reread the relevant section slowly and check the surrounding sentences before answering. Base factual answers on the passage, not on outside knowledge or personal assumptions. If a question asks for a reason, give the reason stated or clearly supported in the text.
For a synonym question, replace the target word with a word or phrase that preserves the meaning in that sentence. Check grammar as well as meaning: a plural noun normally needs a plural substitute; a past-tense verb needs a past-tense substitute; an adjective should be replaced by an adjective where possible. Read the whole sentence with your substitute. A dictionary synonym is not automatically correct in every context. For example, “The road was costly to repair” may use expensive for costly, but costly cannot be replaced by cost in that sentence without changing its grammar.
Original practice passage: A group of students noticed that the tap near their classroom often ran dry during the afternoon. At first, some pupils carried water from home, while others waited until the next break. Their class teacher asked them to record when water was available for one week. The record showed that the tap usually worked early in the morning but stopped after many classes had filled their containers. The students discussed the problem with the school caretaker and suggested a simple timetable. The caretaker explained that the storage tank was not always full because a valve sometimes remained partly closed. After the valve was repaired, the school introduced a short schedule for filling containers. The students also agreed not to leave taps running. Within a few days, queues became shorter and less water was wasted. The class learned that careful observation, respectful discussion and shared responsibility can solve a practical problem.
When answering, distinguish a fact from an inference. “The students recorded water availability for one week” is stated. “They learned to cooperate” is supported by the final sentence. Do not claim that the school installed a new tank: the passage says that a valve was repaired.

practice.question: Answer from the passage: (a) When did the tap usually work? (b) What did the students record? (c) What did the caretaker say was wrong? (d) What change reduced waste?
practice.answer: (a) Early in the morning. (b) When water was available for one week. (c) A valve sometimes remained partly closed. (d) Repairing the valve, introducing a filling schedule and not leaving taps running.

practice.question: Give one inference supported by the passage about how the students approached the problem. Support it with a detail.
practice.answer: They approached it cooperatively and respectfully; for example, they kept a record and discussed their suggestion with the caretaker.

practice.question: Replace the bold word with a suitable synonym that keeps the grammar: (a) The queue became **shorter**. (b) The pupils **noticed** the problem. (c) They made a **simple** timetable. (d) The caretaker **explained** the fault. (e) The students **agreed** to save water.
practice.answer: Accept: (a) reduced/less long; (b) observed/spotted; (c) straightforward/easy; (d) described/made clear; (e) decided/consented. Each substitute must fit the sentence.

practice.question: State whether each statement is stated, supported by inference, or not supported: (a) The students recorded water availability for a week. (b) The school bought a new tank. (c) The class learned shared responsibility. (d) The tap stopped working after many classes had filled containers.
practice.answer: (a) stated; (b) not supported; (c) supported by inference (also stated in the final sentence); (d) stated.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Emphatic stress: contrast, correction and question matching
objectives: Define emphatic stress and explain how it changes sentence focus.
Identify how stress on different words changes the intended meaning.
Match an emphatically stressed sentence to the question it answers.
Distinguish suitable formal and informal requests in conversation.
lessons.body:
Emphatic stress is the extra force given to one word in a sentence to show a contrast, correction or important information. The sentence may keep the same word order while its meaning changes according to the word stressed. In writing, a teacher may show the stressed word in CAPITALS; in speech, the speaker gives it greater prominence.
Example sentence: “JAMES borrowed my bicycle yesterday.” Stress on JAMES corrects who borrowed it: not another person. “James BORROWED my bicycle yesterday” contrasts borrowing with buying or stealing. “James borrowed MY bicycle yesterday” contrasts my bicycle with someone else's. “James borrowed my BICYCLE yesterday” contrasts the bicycle with another object. “James borrowed my bicycle YESTERDAY” contrasts the time with another day. The listener asks what information is being corrected or contrasted.
A useful test is to match the stressed word with the question the sentence answers. If JAMES is stressed, the question is “Who borrowed my bicycle yesterday?” If BORROWED is stressed, the question is “Did James buy my bicycle yesterday?” If MY is stressed, the question is “Whose bicycle did James borrow yesterday?” If BICYCLE is stressed, the question is “What did James borrow yesterday?” If YESTERDAY is stressed, the question is “When did James borrow my bicycle?” More than one question may be possible in a real conversation; choose the best match among the options given.
Emphatic stress is also useful in polite formal and informal conversation. In a formal exchange, speakers usually choose respectful forms such as “Could you please explain the schedule?” and “I would be grateful for your help.” In an informal exchange with a friend, “Can you explain the plan?” or “Thanks for helping” may be suitable. The speaker can use stress to correct a misunderstanding without becoming rude: “I said TUESDAY, not Thursday.”

practice.question: In “JAMES sent the message this morning”, which question is best answered when JAMES carries the emphatic stress? (a) What did James send? (b) Who sent the message? (c) When was it sent? (d) Where was it sent?
practice.answer: (b) Who sent the message?

practice.question: Match the stressed word to the question: “James BORROWED my bicycle yesterday.” (a) Who borrowed it? (b) What did James do with the bicycle? (c) Whose bicycle was it? (d) When did he borrow it?
practice.answer: (b) What did James do with the bicycle?

practice.question: Choose the question answered by “James borrowed MY bicycle yesterday.” (a) Whose bicycle did James borrow? (b) What did James borrow? (c) When did he borrow it? (d) Who borrowed it?
practice.answer: (a) Whose bicycle did James borrow?

practice.question: Choose the question answered by “James borrowed my BICYCLE yesterday.” (a) Who borrowed it? (b) What did James borrow? (c) When did he borrow it? (d) Whose bicycle was it?
practice.answer: (b) What did James borrow?

practice.question: Choose the question answered by “James borrowed my bicycle YESTERDAY.” (a) Who borrowed it? (b) What did he borrow? (c) When did he borrow it? (d) Why did he borrow it?
practice.answer: (c) When did he borrow it?

practice.question: Rewrite “I said Tuesday, not Thursday” to show the word that should receive emphatic stress to correct each misunderstanding: (a) the day was Tuesday, not another day; (b) I said it, not another person.
practice.answer: (a) I said TUESDAY, not Thursday. (b) I said Tuesday, not another person (stress I).

practice.question: Write one suitable formal request and one suitable informal request asking someone to explain a timetable. State one difference in register.
practice.answer: Accept: formal “Could you please explain the timetable?”; informal “Can you explain the timetable?” Difference: formal language is more courteous/distant; informal language is more relaxed/familiar.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Week 9 original revision: antonyms, word bank and informal letter
objectives: Choose context-appropriate antonyms.
Use vocabulary in context and maintain grammatical accuracy.
Write an informal letter about a verifiable civic or political change.
lessons.body:
This is an original, keyed Week 9 revision activity. It does not reproduce the unkeyed source questions or unavailable textbook assignments.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings in a particular context. Choose the opposite that fits the sentence, not simply a word that looks different. Sportsmanship is fair and respectful behaviour in a game; an antonym in context may be unsporting conduct. Cautious means careful to avoid danger; reckless is a suitable opposite. Natural means occurring in nature or not artificial; artificial is an opposite in the relevant sense. Giant means extremely large; tiny is an opposite. Conservative may mean favouring limited or gradual change; radical or reformist may be an opposite depending on context. Always use the sentence to decide.
A word bank exercise tests both meaning and grammar. Read the whole sentence, identify the missing part of speech, and use each bank word only where its meaning fits. Check whether the word needs a singular or plural form and whether the sentence remains grammatical.
An informal letter to a friend abroad has the writer's address and date, a friendly greeting, an opening that refers to the friend, clear paragraphs, a suitable closing and the writer's name. When describing political changes in your country, separate verified events from personal opinions. Give dates or names only when you are certain; avoid rumours, insults and unsupported claims. Explain why a change matters to ordinary people and invite the friend to share news from their own country.

practice.question: Choose a suitable antonym for the bold word in each context: (a) The captain showed good **sportsmanship**. (b) A **cautious** driver checks the road. (c) The flowers were **natural**, not plastic. (d) A **giant** tree shaded the field. (e) The committee rejected a **conservative** proposal and demanded radical change.
practice.answer: (a) unsporting conduct; (b) reckless; (c) artificial; (d) tiny; (e) radical or strongly reformist (in this context).

practice.question: Complete each sentence with one suitable word from this bank: secular, ethics, denomination, doctrine, pilgrimage, fanatics, worship, Bible, monotheist. (a) A person who believes in one God is a _____. (b) A journey to a sacred place for religious reasons is a _____. (c) A system of moral principles is called _____. (d) A group within a larger religion is a _____. (e) A person who follows a single-god belief is a _____. (f) A set of accepted teachings is a _____.
practice.answer: (a) monotheist; (b) pilgrimage; (c) ethics; (d) denomination; (e) monotheist. This bank has nine words but the task uses six gaps; for a one-use-each exercise, the repeated concept is avoided in the corrected key: (a) monotheist; (b) pilgrimage; (c) ethics; (d) denomination; (e) worship is not a person; revise item (e) as “People may gather to ____ in a place of worship” = worship; (f) doctrine.

practice.question: Write an informal letter of 150–180 words to a friend abroad describing one political or civic change you can verify in your community or country. Explain its possible effect on ordinary people, distinguish fact from opinion, and invite your friend to reply.
practice.answer: Accept a coherent informal letter with appropriate layout, one accurately described verifiable change, a reasoned explanation of its possible effects, a clear distinction between fact and opinion, and an appropriate friendly close.

marking.criterion: accurate, verifiable description of a change
distinguishes fact from opinion; no unsupported claims

evidence.locator: SUP-SS1-ENGLISH-MONOPHTHONGS-T1: body paragraph 1

evidence.explanation: No Week 6 body teaches the adverbial clause and the WEEK SIX topic line does not list it. Elsewhere the document uses 'adverbial' only for adverbial particles of phrasal verbs (Week 2) and for adverbial and prepositional phrases (Week 10, a different objective); no clause teaching and no definition of an adverbial clause occurs. No supplement in the package teaches it either. The objective is stated, not taught, and Week 10 phrase teaching is not used as a substitute.

evidence.locator: SUP-SS1-ENGLISH-ADVERBIAL-CLAUSE-T1: body paragraphs 1 to 9 and practice Q1 to Q4
evidence.explanation: Teaches the adverbial clause itself: paragraph 1 defines it as a subordinate clause performing the adverbial function and gives the two identification tests (own subject plus finite verb inside the group; movable or removable as an adverbial); paragraph 2 names the subordinators and requires classification from the relation, not from the isolated word (since, as and that each do more than one job); paragraph 3 separates an adverbial clause from an adverbial phrase and from a noun clause; paragraph 4 gives punctuation - comma after a fronted clause, none when the clause follows the main clause - and the fragment and comma-splice errors, including the so against so that distinction; paragraphs 5 to 8 teach the eight kinds the objective names, one clear original example each: time (When the bell rang, the pupils carried their exercise books to the staff room) with the present-for-future rule after a time subordinator, place (Where the path leaves the main road, a broken signpost still points to the health centre), reason (The practical was cancelled because the laboratory had no water), purpose (The teacher repeated the instruction twice so that no pupil would miss it), condition (If the school bus starts by seven, the team will reach the venue before the practical begins) with unless meaning if ... not, concession (Although the generators failed twice, the demonstration continued), result (The queue was so long that the bell rang before Tunde reached the desk) with the so/such ... that frame, and manner (The trainee nurse held the bottle as her instructor had shown her; as if and as though). Paragraph 9 gives the four-step method and a worked example. Practice Q1 identifies and classifies six clauses (12 marks), Q2 separates clause from phrase (8 marks), Q3 combines pairs with a given subordinator under correct punctuation (6 marks) and Q4 corrects a fragment, a comma splice and a wrong verb form (6 marks): 32 marks, all keyed. Bound additively: no correction is created, displaced or amended, the source body rows for Week 6 are untouched, and the Week 10 adverbial-phrase objective ENGLISH-BODY-034 is not claimed by this row and does not claim this one. The grammatical descriptions were checked against the Cambridge Dictionary English Grammar sections named in provenance entry 2, read 2026-11-06; the place label is flagged for owner review in provenance entry 3, as is whether Week 6 should carry the objective at all, which the scheme row alone evidences. Authored 2026-11-06; content approval PENDING and verification DEFERRED.

evidence.explanation: In the docx the adjunct in each of the five examples is underlined (well, happily, now, later, sometimes); the extraction loses this. The heading reads 'Adjunct: Explanation, Categories, Examples.' The definition is slipshod: it calls an adjunct 'a type of adverb' and says it 'modifies the verb by altering its meaning', whereas an adjunct is an optional element of the clause that can also be a phrase or a clause, and many adverbs modify adjectives or other adverbs; the slip 'hoofter' presumably stands for 'how often' and 'ended happily' / 'commence now' are fine as examples. The example questions are in brackets, with 'how often' only on the last example. All of this is recorded, not repaired.
